newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans regulators to woo funds in power units.
newsitem.headline: India plans regulators to woo funds in power units.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said on Friday that the government was planning to set up regulatory authorities to attract foreign investment into the power sector through transparent procedures.

"The government is looking at the possibility of introducing legal changes to set up regulatory authorities at the central (federal) and state levels," he said at the conclusion of a seminar on the power sector.

The government was also keen to reduce losses resulting from inefficiency in transmission and distribution of electricity and will make legal changes to attract private investment in power distribution, Deve Gowda said.

India's attempts to attract private and foreign investments to meet a huge shortfall in power has met with roadblocks linked to political and public criticism over an early round of projects concluded through negotiated contracts.

The criticism has centred around a perceived lack of transparency, the price to be paid for power bought by state-run distribution companies, environmental regulations and cost of generation of power.
The government was promoting the practice of competitive bidding to attract private investment to set up power generation capacities, Deve Gowda said.
The demand for power was growing by an average of nine percent every year, and India needed to add 142,000 megawatts of power generation capacity by 2007, he said.
Officials say roughly 40 million rupees ($1.1 million) are needed to create one megawatt of capacity.

Deve Gowda said he would convene a meeting of state chief ministers to discuss the question of reforming loss-making state electricity boards (SEBs) and discuss a shortfall in power generation. He did not mention any date.
"We are strongly on the reform and liberalisation route," Deve Gowda said. "We have to cover a large ground."

India is welcoming foreign investors in the power sector under a five-year-old economic reform programme, but the poor financial health of the SEBs, who would pay for the electricity generated, worries investors.
Deve Gowda assured private power producers, who made recommendations to the government at the end of the seminar, that he would seriously consider their demands.

They asked for an automatic approval of power projects that will cost up to 40 billion rupees. Currently, all power projects requiring investments of more than 10 billion rupees needs a techno-economic approval from the government.
